newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's annual trade surplus falls sharply.
newsitem.headline: Japan's annual trade surplus falls sharply.

text.p: Japan's trade surplus, long a political issue with its major trading partners, fell nearly a third last year, but data also showed a rising surplus with the United States.
Figures released by the Finance Ministry on Thursday showed the customs-cleared trade surplus for 1996 was down 32.4 percent at 6.74 trillion yen ($56.6 billion).
The surplus with the United States declined 16.5 percent to 3.55 trillion yen ($29.8 billion).
But the figures for December alone showed that the surplus with the United States is again rising, climbing 7.8 percent from a year earlier to 389.11 billion yen ($3.26 billion).
The overall surplus in December fell 20.6 percent from a year earlier to 881.48 billion yen ($7.40 billion).
Economists polled by Reuters had predicted an average fall of about 7.4 percent to 1.029 trillion yen ($8.6 billion) for the overall December figure.

The trade surplus has been pushed down in reaction to a strong Japanese yen, which climbed to a level of around 80 to the dollar in April 1995. Since then, however, the yen has been falling sharply and on Thursday was at 119 yen per dollar.
Analysts said that the fall in the yen will likely send the trade surplus heading back up.

"I think the overall trade figure will continue to increase rather than decline because the weaker Japanese yen would really help boost exports, especially automobiles," said Satoshi Shimamoto, senior economist at MMS International.
But some analysts said they did not think a rising surplus would pose new problems for U.S.-Japan ties.

Naofumi Kinoshita, vice president at First Chicago in Tokyo, said he doubted the administration of President Bill Clinton was focused on the trade balance and noted that the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations have said they are agreed on a "strong dollar" policy.
The financial markets showed little reaction to the figures. The stock market, which has been tumbling since early December, was little changed in morning trading.

The yen hit the latest in a string of near four-year lows against the dollar, but traders said this was due mainly to the dollar's overall strength against other currencies rather than any new worries about the yen.
The Finance Ministry also revised its trade figures for November to show a marginal fall in the overall surplus, rather than a slight rise as previously announced.

It said the surplus fell a revised 0.4 percent in November to 670.77 billion yen ($5.63 billion), compared to the original figure released on December 18 of 675.19 billion yen ($5.67 billion), which would have been the first rise in the surplus in two years.
The figures cover merchandise trade. Japan announces data for the current account, a broader measure of trade including services such as tourism, separately. ($1=119 yen)
